title: A 5% Down Payment Needs a Cash Buffer
meta_description: A practical U.S. framework for judging a 5% home down payment through cash to close, mortgage insurance, monthly costs, repairs, reserves and equity risk.

module_headings.internal_links: Internal Links: Related Daily Yield Resources

sections.heading: Five Percent Down Is an Entry Point, Not an Affordability Test
paragraphs: A five-percent down payment can move a buyer into a home sooner, preserve years otherwise spent saving and make a purchase possible in a rising market. It can also leave the buyer with a larger loan, mortgage insurance, little equity and too little cash for repairs. The percentage alone cannot identify a ladder or a trap.

The opening photograph shows buyers reviewing real-estate documents because the decision lives in the full transaction. For a $400,000 home, five percent is $20,000. That is not the same as cash to close, and it says nothing about the monthly payment, taxes, insurance, association dues, maintenance or reserves remaining afterward.

A lender’s approval tests the loan against underwriting rules. A household must perform a broader test covering childcare, health costs, transportation, retirement, job risk and the property’s condition. Approval is not an instruction to spend the maximum.

Low-down-payment mortgages are not inherently irresponsible. Qualified conventional, FHA, VA and USDA options can responsibly expand access. Their eligibility, fees, insurance and occupancy rules differ. Compare actual Loan Estimates rather than assuming one label always wins.
The core rule is simple: a down payment succeeds only when the closing leaves enough monthly and liquid capacity to own the property safely.

Use a decision sheet with four gates. First, can the buyer close without borrowing the cash? Second, does the payment work on dependable income? Third, will adequate reserves remain? Fourth, is the expected holding period long enough to tolerate selling friction? A failure at any gate calls for a cheaper home, more saving or delay—not optimistic arithmetic.

Separate ability from preference. A buyer may be able to carry the mortgage yet prefer mobility, retirement contributions or a shorter commute. Renting can be a rational purchase of flexibility. Buying can be rational when tenure, control and a suitable holding period justify the costs. The framework does not need a universal winner for every buyer, city or economic cycle.

Write the decision rule before emotion and competition enter the offer. Record the maximum price, maximum verified monthly cost, minimum reserve balance and unacceptable property risks. Share those limits with any co-buyer. If an offer violates one limit, change the offer rather than rewriting the policy. This protects against escalation when another bidder, an expiring lease or a persuasive sales conversation creates urgency.

sections.heading: Build Cash to Close Before Choosing a Percentage
paragraphs: Cash to close can include the down payment, lender and third-party charges, prepaid interest, initial escrow deposits, homeowner’s insurance, taxes and adjustments, minus deposits, seller credits and other allowed credits. The figure changes with price, timing and loan structure.

The CFPB [[S1|home-loan toolkit]] explains that borrowers should be prepared for the full cash-to-close amount and should compare the Closing Disclosure with the selected Loan Estimate. Keep both documents and ask about every change.
Create separate buckets for down payment, estimated closing costs, moving, immediate repairs and post-closing reserves. Do not present one savings balance as available for all five purposes.

Earnest money is typically credited in the transaction but may be at risk under contract terms. Understand financing, appraisal, inspection and sale contingencies with qualified local help before transferring funds.
Obtain updated figures before making an offer and again before closing. A rate change, tax estimate, insurance quote or closing date can alter cash and payment.

Run a cash-to-close rehearsal thirty days before the planned offer. Put the down payment and estimated closing cash in a separate insured account, preserve the reserve floor and live on the proposed post-purchase budget. If ordinary spending repeatedly invades either amount, the proposed transaction is not ready.

Wire fraud is a closing risk. Independently verify transfer instructions using a trusted telephone number obtained before any urgent email. Never rely only on a last-minute message changing account details. Ask the settlement professional about secure procedures and immediately contact the bank and relevant parties if anything appears wrong.

Distinguish closing funds from reserves on every update. If an estimate rises, do not quietly reduce the emergency fund to preserve the target price. Instead identify whether the increase is a corrected cost, a timing item, an optional point or a genuine affordability warning. Re-price the home, negotiate permitted credits or pause. A transparent adjustment is safer than allowing the reserve balance to become an unexplained plug number.

Create a closing ledger with columns for the latest estimate, who pays, when it is due, whether it is refundable and the source document. Include inspection, appraisal and other pre-closing spending even if those amounts are absent from final cash to close. Reconcile the ledger weekly. This prevents already-paid costs from vanishing from the affordability analysis and makes a failed transaction’s sunk costs visible before the household immediately pursues another property.

sections.heading: Compare Five, Ten and Twenty Percent Honestly
paragraphs: A larger down payment reduces the loan balance and usually the principal-and-interest payment. It can affect pricing and mortgage insurance. But moving from five to twenty percent may consume years of liquidity or delay the purchase. Compare scenarios with the same home, rate date, term and cost assumptions.

For a $400,000 home, five percent is $20,000, ten percent is $40,000 and twenty percent is $80,000. The loan balances before financed fees would be $380,000, $360,000 and $320,000. The $60,000 difference between five and twenty percent must be weighed against payment savings, insurance, interest and cash retained.

Do not assume retained cash will earn a specific investment return. Its first job may be emergency resilience and repairs. Likewise, do not call home equity lost money; it reduces leverage but is less liquid and costly to access.

Ask the lender for written side-by-side Loan Estimates or equivalent scenarios. Compare interest rate, annual percentage rate, points, mortgage insurance, total monthly payment, cash to close and five-year cost—not only principal and interest.
Choose the percentage after the reserve test, not before it.

The correct comparison can change by price tier. Twenty percent down on a home requiring immediate systems work may be weaker than ten percent on a sound, less expensive property with reserves. Negotiate the house, financing and cash position as one system rather than maximizing a single ratio.

Include opportunity costs without pretending they are certain. Cash used for the down payment cannot simultaneously fund retirement, eliminate expensive debt or protect against unemployment. Cash retained also has a cost because the mortgage is larger. State assumed savings yield, tax treatment and risk rather than hiding them.

Compare the incremental step, not only the endpoints. Moving from five to ten percent may alter insurance pricing or rate; moving from ten to fifteen can produce another result. Ask for scenarios rather than extrapolating. The best point may be between five and twenty, but only if it preserves the reserve floor. Round percentages are convenient labels, not financial objectives.

sections.heading: Mortgage Insurance Protects the Lender
paragraphs: The CFPB [[S2|explains]] that borrowers putting less than twenty percent down commonly pay mortgage insurance. It reduces lender risk and can enable approval, but it adds borrower cost. Terms differ between conventional PMI and government mortgage insurance.

Conventional PMI pricing can vary with credit, loan-to-value and other factors. It may be monthly, upfront or lender-paid through pricing. “No PMI” does not necessarily mean no cost; compare rate, fees and second-lien terms.

FHA loans require FHA mortgage insurance, including upfront and annual components under applicable rules. Do not compare an FHA headline rate with a conventional rate while omitting insurance and financed upfront cost.

VA-backed loans generally do not require monthly mortgage insurance but can carry a funding fee unless exempt. USDA programs have their own guarantee and annual fees. Eligibility and property rules matter.
Record when and how each insurance cost can end. A low initial payment can become less attractive if insurance lasts longer than expected.

Ask for the insurance amount in dollars and the assumptions behind it. Model the payment before and after expected cancellation, but make the purchase work at the higher amount. A future reduction is a planning benefit, not permission to accept an unaffordable opening payment.

Read the program-specific disclosures. Conventional PMI cancellation rights described here generally concern borrower-paid PMI on covered mortgages and include conditions and exceptions. Government mortgage insurance follows separate rules. A servicer or housing counselor can clarify the actual loan; a generic calculator cannot amend the note.

Include mortgage insurance in the holding-period calculation. Estimate total premiums over three, five and seven years under the quoted structure, then show the possible cancellation point separately. Do not present that date as guaranteed if it depends on payments, value, seasoning or servicer evidence. This turns a vague dislike of PMI into a measurable cost that can be weighed against earlier ownership and retained cash.

sections.heading: Test the Full Monthly Housing Payment
paragraphs: Principal and interest are only the center of the payment. Add property taxes, homeowner’s insurance, mortgage insurance, flood or wind coverage where relevant, association dues, special assessments and utilities. Escrow estimates can change after closing.

Use current insurance quotes for the specific property. A prior owner’s premium, listing estimate or regional average may not reflect the buyer, roof, claims history or hazard exposure. If coverage is difficult to obtain, investigate before contingency deadlines.

Property taxes may reset after sale or lose a prior owner’s exemption. Review local rules and recent assessments. A lender’s initial escrow can underestimate the later payment if it relies on old tax data.
Stress-test a twenty-percent tax or insurance increase, one income interruption and association assessment. If the payment only works under the first-year estimate, the home is not safely affordable.
Set an internal payment ceiling from dependable net income and other goals. Debt-to-income approval ratios are not household budgets.

Build a twelve-month payment table. Show principal and interest separately from every item that can change. Include an annual-to-monthly reserve for costs not escrowed. This prevents the low advertised mortgage payment from becoming the household’s affordability number.

Test payment reliability against net income, not a strong gross-income month. For commissions, bonuses, overtime or self-employment, use conservative dependable cash flow and preserve more liquidity. A second income should not be counted at full strength if childcare, leave or schedule constraints can interrupt it.

Account for costs paid outside escrow. Association dues, water, trash, flood policies, maintenance contracts and special taxing districts may not appear in the lender’s estimated total. Review listing documents, public records and association materials with appropriate professionals. A cost omitted from escrow remains a household obligation, and an annual bill should be divided into monthly saving before the payment is judged affordable.

Budget for payment timing as well as amount. The first mortgage payment may not arrive immediately, but prepaid interest and moving bills can cluster around closing. Do not interpret a delayed first payment as free cash. Map the final rent payment, deposits, overlapping utilities, mortgage start date and credit-card statement cycles. A short overlap can be prudent; an unplanned overlap can consume the repair reserve before the household understands its new recurring costs.

sections.heading: The Repair Fund Begins on Closing Day
paragraphs: The midpoint photograph shows major home renovation because ownership transfers repair risk immediately. A five-percent down payment creates no exemption from a failed roof, water heater, sewer line, appliance or electrical problem. New construction also needs maintenance and may carry exclusions or delays under warranties.

Obtain an independent inspection permitted by the contract and use qualified specialists when concerns arise. An inspection is not a guarantee, and a lender appraisal is not a condition report for the buyer.

Estimate near-term work by urgency: safety and water intrusion, essential systems, deterioration prevention and cosmetic preference. Get quotes where possible before closing. Do not fund cosmetic projects while a known essential risk remains unreserved.
Maintain a post-closing repair reserve separate from general emergencies. The amount should reflect age, condition, systems, climate, deductible and ability to perform safe work.
A low-down-payment purchase becomes fragile when every repair must go onto expensive credit.

A useful reserve estimate is property-specific, not a universal percentage. List the age and plausible replacement window of roof, heating and cooling, plumbing, electrical service, appliances and exterior components. Add insurance deductibles and urgent items identified during inspection. Revisit the list annually.

Seller repairs and credits require judgment. A credit preserves closing speed but leaves execution risk with the buyer; a repair may be rushed or poorly documented. Contract rules and lender limits vary. Use qualified local professionals, written scopes, permits where required and final verification.

Inspection findings also affect insurance and financing. Roof age, electrical panels, prior damage or incomplete work can influence coverage, required repairs and closing feasibility. Obtain specialist advice and quotes within contract deadlines. If the seller will not address a severe issue, walking away under a valid contingency can preserve far more wealth than using every reserve dollar to rescue a marginal purchase.

sections.heading: Small Equity Magnifies Price and Selling Risk
paragraphs: With five percent down, transaction costs and a modest price decline can erase apparent equity. Equity is market value minus debts secured by the home, not simply the original down payment plus every monthly payment.

Early mortgage payments are weighted toward interest under a standard amortizing loan, so principal can fall slowly. Check the amortization schedule rather than assuming one year of payments creates one year’s worth of substantial equity.

Selling costs can consume proceeds through brokerage, concessions, repairs, transfer charges and moving. A buyer expecting to relocate soon needs a break-even analysis, not a claim that rent is always wasted.

Model a five-percent price decline and sale after two, five and seven years. Use conservative selling costs and no guaranteed appreciation. Flexibility has value when employment or family location may change.
Leverage amplifies the owner’s percentage gain when prices rise and loss when prices fall. That is a risk feature, not a prediction.

Negative equity does not automatically create a crisis if the owner can afford the home and does not need to sell. The danger is the combination of low equity with a forced move, income loss, major repair or unaffordable payment. Reserves and a suitable holding period reduce that combination risk.

Do not count renovation spending dollar for dollar as market value. Some work preserves condition; some reflects taste; some can be necessary without raising resale price by its cost. Buy for utility within a resilient budget, and treat appreciation as uncertain rather than as the repair fund.

Calculate a sale-resilience number: conservative value minus estimated selling costs, mortgage payoff and any assistance lien. Repeat it after a five-percent decline. This is not a forecast; it reveals how much cash an early move could require. A household with likely relocation should demand more liquidity or a lower price because a strong monthly budget does not remove transaction friction.

sections.heading: Low-Down-Payment Programs Are Not Interchangeable
paragraphs: Freddie Mac [[S3|HomeOne]] and other eligible conventional products can permit qualified buyers to put as little as three percent down. FHA can allow a minimum required investment of 3.5 percent for eligible transactions. VA and USDA programs can permit no down payment for eligible borrowers and properties.

Minimum down payment does not mean minimum cash needed, automatic approval or lowest lifetime cost. Programs differ in income, occupancy, first-time-buyer, geography, property, education, fee and underwriting rules.

Down-payment assistance may be a grant, forgivable loan, deferred loan or repayable second mortgage. Read repayment triggers tied to sale, refinance, move-out or time. Add every lien when calculating equity.
Compare program restrictions with likely plans. A home that fails property standards or a buyer who may move soon can face different practical costs.
Use a HUD-approved housing counselor or qualified lender to explore eligibility, then independently compare offers.

For VA, the official [[S5|purchase-loan guidance]] says eligible borrowers can often buy with no down payment when price does not exceed appraised value and that a funding fee may apply, while monthly mortgage insurance is generally absent. For USDA, eligible applicants and properties face income and geographic conditions and program fees. Verify current rules directly.

FHA may compete well for some credit profiles while conventional financing may compete better for others. Assistance can change cash needs yet add a second lien. Request the same price, term, lock period and closing date across scenarios so program names do not hide economic differences.

Housing counselors can help interpret choices, but buyers remain responsible for checking credentials and documents. A real-estate agent, lender, inspector, appraiser, attorney and counselor have different roles and incentives. Ask each professional what they do not cover. Coordinated advice is useful; substituting one professional’s opinion for another discipline can leave title, condition, insurance or loan risks unexamined.

sections.heading: Shop the Mortgage, Not Just the House
paragraphs: Request Loan Estimates from multiple lenders within a focused period using matching assumptions. Compare rate, points, lender credits, origination charges, mortgage insurance, projected payment, cash to close and services that can be shopped.

A lender credit usually exchanges lower upfront cash for a higher rate or other pricing. Discount points exchange upfront cash for a lower rate. Calculate break-even against the realistic holding period rather than treating either as free.
Rate locks have duration and conditions. Ask what happens if closing is delayed, rates fall or loan details change. Confirm extension cost and responsibility.
Do not let a seller’s preferred lender or a real-estate deadline end comparison. Incentives can be valuable, but compare net economics and service reliability.
Keep written estimates and refuse to sign documents not understood. The final Closing Disclosure should be reconciled line by line.

Examine page one and the comparisons section, then page two line items. Ask which services can be shopped, whether quoted third parties are realistic and whether taxes and insurance are current. A lower rate paired with high points may not win over the expected holding period.

Service quality has financial value when contracts have deadlines, but it should be verified rather than merely promised. Ask who handles underwriting, how appraisal issues are escalated and what documentation remains outstanding. Keep a timeline and send sensitive records only through verified secure channels.

Treat each lender scenario as a package. A low rate can be paired with points; a credit can be paired with a higher rate; low cash can be paired with financed fees. Compare total dollars over the expected holding period and the amount due at closing. Then examine risk: adjustable features, balloon payments, prepayment terms or subordinate financing deserve explicit explanation before acceptance.

sections.heading: Keep the Cash Buffer After the Keys
paragraphs: A buyer should leave closing with operating cash, an emergency reserve and property-specific repair money. The same dollar cannot serve all three. Set minimum post-closing balances before establishing the offer ceiling.

Operating cash covers timing between escrow, utilities, moving and ordinary bills. Emergency savings covers income or serious household shocks. Repair reserves address ownership risks. Furnishing is a separate, flexible category.
Avoid opening new credit or financing furniture before closing because it can change underwriting. Continue following lender instructions and disclose required financial changes.
After closing, resist filling every room immediately. Live in the property, learn its systems and fund safety work first. Cash preserved at closing buys time to make better choices.
If five percent down leaves reserves intact while twenty percent empties them, the smaller down payment may be safer despite higher loan cost. If neither leaves reserves, the price is too high.

Define the reserve floor in dollars and months before touring. For example, calculate essential non-housing expenses plus the new housing payment, then decide how many months must remain based on employment stability, dependents, insurance deductibles and property condition. This is a household policy, not a lender minimum.

Gifts can help where program rules allow, but document them as required and avoid informal repayment promises that create undisclosed debt. Likewise, do not assume a future tax refund, bonus or family contribution will repair a weak closing position. Funds should be verified and seasoned or sourced according to lender requirements.

The reserve target should rise when income is concentrated in one job, the household has dependents, the property is older or insurance deductibles are large. It may also need to cover a gap between job loss and benefit eligibility. There is no single correct month count, but there must be an explicit dollar amount supported by the household’s actual risks rather than whatever remains after closing.

sections.heading: Create an Exit From Mortgage Insurance
paragraphs: For many conventional mortgages, federal law gives eligible borrowers rights around PMI cancellation. The CFPB [[S4|states]] that a borrower can generally request cancellation when scheduled or actual principal reaches eighty percent of original value, subject to conditions, and automatic termination generally occurs at seventy-eight percent when current.

Keep the PMI disclosure and amortization schedule. Calendar the earliest request date and servicer requirements. Additional principal can change actual balance, but verify whether an appraisal or certification is required.

FHA mortgage insurance cancellation rules differ by loan terms and origination conditions; refinancing may be one route but introduces qualification, rate and closing costs. Never assume refinancing will be available or beneficial.
Do not make extra principal payments that deplete emergency cash solely to remove PMI. Compare guaranteed interest and insurance savings with liquidity needs.
When insurance ends, redirect the payment toward reserves, principal, retirement or another written goal rather than letting it disappear.

A cancellation strategy should include the exact original value used under the applicable rules, scheduled balance, request method and evidence. Market appreciation may support different investor or servicer options in some cases, but it is not the same as the federal original-value timetable. Ask for written requirements before ordering an appraisal.

Refinancing solely to remove insurance deserves a full break-even analysis. Compare new rate, term reset, points, title and settlement charges with remaining insurance and interest. A smaller payment can still cost more if the term is extended. Do not convert an expected cancellation into unnecessary closing costs.

When considering extra principal, compare three balances: emergency reserves, known repair sinking funds and the mortgage. Sending cash to principal is difficult to reverse without a new loan or sale. A borrower with weak liquid reserves may benefit more from rebuilding cash first, even though principal reduction offers a certain interest saving. Liquidity and net worth are related but not interchangeable.

sections.heading: Move In Without Becoming House-Poor
paragraphs: The late photograph shows a family unpacking because closing begins homeownership rather than completing the financial work. Update the household budget with actual payment, utilities, commuting, maintenance and insurance. Compare with estimates after three and twelve months.

Create a home file with deed and title records, loan documents, Closing Disclosure, inspection, warranties, insurance, tax notices, association rules and contractor receipts. Protect digital and physical copies.

Schedule seasonal maintenance and save monthly for known replacements. Track property condition, not just market value. Equity cannot fix a leak before it damages the house unless cash or affordable credit is available.
Review beneficiaries, liability coverage and estate documents when ownership changes household risk. Unmarried co-buyers should obtain local legal advice on title, contributions, exit and death.

A five-percent down payment becomes a ladder when it secures a suitable home while preserving monthly margin, repairs, reserves and holding flexibility. It becomes a trap when qualification replaces planning and the keys arrive with no cash left.

During the first year, use a monthly ownership review: actual payment, escrow changes, utility trend, maintenance performed, reserve balance and upcoming large work. The objective is not constant worry; it is early detection while choices remain available.

If hardship occurs, contact the servicer early and seek a HUD-approved housing counselor. Options depend on the loan and circumstances. Avoid companies demanding large upfront fees or guaranteeing a modification. Keep records of calls, submissions and deadlines, and continue opening all mail.

Homeownership should support the household’s life rather than dominate it. Continue retirement saving at an intentional level, protect essential insurance and leave room for recurring family needs. If the first realistic budget requires permanent overtime, skipped health care or new revolving debt, the purchase price is too aggressive. A durable home plan works during ordinary imperfect months, not only under peak earnings and zero surprises.

Set annual review triggers instead of reacting to every housing headline. Review insurance before renewal, taxes after assessment, mortgage insurance eligibility on its scheduled date and estate or ownership documents after a family change. Re-shop coverage without creating gaps. The house price on a website does not need monthly attention; cash flow, maintenance and adequate protection do. These controls make low-equity ownership progressively stronger without relying on speculative appreciation.

summary: Five percent down is an entry structure, not proof that a home is affordable. Evaluate the complete transaction and the household that must sustain it.
Calculate cash to close separately from the down payment. Include lender charges, third-party costs, prepaids, escrow funding, credits, deposits and adjustments.
Create distinct buckets for closing, moving, urgent repairs, operating cash and emergencies. The same dollar cannot be assigned to several jobs.
Compare five, ten and twenty percent using the same home, rate date, term and holding period. Measure payment, insurance, interest, fees and liquidity retained.
Test the full monthly cost: principal, interest, taxes, homeowner’s insurance, mortgage insurance, association charges, utilities and maintenance reserves.
Use current property-specific insurance quotes and local tax information. Escrow payments can rise after purchase when taxes or premiums change.
Mortgage insurance protects the lender, not the buyer. Compare conventional PMI, FHA insurance, VA funding fees and USDA fees under the actual offer.
Preserve property-specific repair cash after inspection. An appraisal does not replace an inspection, and a new home is not maintenance-free.
Model price declines and selling costs. Five percent equity can be consumed quickly, especially when a move occurs early in the loan.
Compare eligible conventional, FHA, VA, USDA and assistance programs by complete economics and restrictions, not their minimum down payment.
Shop multiple Loan Estimates with matching assumptions. Compare points, credits, APR, insurance, projected payments, cash to close and five-year cost.
Reconcile the selected Loan Estimate with the Closing Disclosure and ask about every change before signing documents not understood.
Define a post-closing reserve floor before establishing the home-price ceiling. If neither five nor twenty percent preserves it, reduce price or delay.
Plan an exit from conventional PMI using the disclosure, amortization schedule and servicer rules, but do not drain emergency cash merely to cancel it.
Treat appreciation and refinancing as uncertain. The purchase must work without either outcome.
Choose a holding period compatible with job and family plans. Renting can rationally preserve flexibility when an early move is plausible.
After moving in, track actual housing costs, escrow, utilities, repairs and reserves. Delay optional furnishing until the property and budget are understood.
A five-percent down payment is a ladder when it preserves monthly margin, reserves and flexibility. It is a trap when closing consumes all available cash.
Write maximum price, verified monthly-cost ceiling and minimum reserve balance before making offers. Do not relax all three because a property attracts competing bids.
Run a closing rehearsal by separating expected closing money and living on the proposed ownership budget. Repeatedly invading the reserve is a warning to adjust.
Use an independent inspection when permitted and specialists for serious concerns. Seller credits, repairs and walk-away rights depend on contracts and professional local advice.
Calculate sale resilience as conservative value minus selling costs, mortgage payoff and assistance liens. Repeat after a modest price decline to expose forced-move risk.
Keep conventional PMI disclosures and calendar possible cancellation dates, but distinguish federal original-value rules from any separate investor treatment of appreciation.
Treat points and lender credits as pricing exchanges, not gifts. Compare their break-even period with how long the household realistically expects to keep the loan.
Independently verify wire instructions through a trusted contact method. Last-minute emailed changes can be fraud and should never be followed without direct confirmation.
Raise the reserve target for variable income, dependents, older property systems or large deductibles. A lender minimum is not a household resilience standard.

Keep a property file containing the Loan Estimate, Closing Disclosure, inspection, insurance, tax records, warranties and maintenance history. Review actual ownership costs after three and twelve months, then revise monthly saving for repairs and annual bills.

faq.question: Is five percent down financially irresponsible?
faq.answer: No. It can be sensible when the full payment is affordable, the property fits the holding period and adequate cash remains after closing.

faq.question: Does five percent down mean I only need five percent in cash?
faq.answer: No. Closing costs, prepaids, escrows, moving, repairs and post-closing reserves can require substantial additional cash.

faq.question: Will conventional PMI disappear automatically?
faq.answer: Covered loans generally have cancellation and automatic-termination rights subject to rules and conditions. Keep the disclosure and ask the servicer for the loan-specific dates.

faq.question: Is twenty percent always safer?
faq.answer: Not if it empties emergency and repair reserves. Compare the smaller loan with the liquidity sacrificed.

faq.question: Does an appraisal show the home is in good condition?
faq.answer: No. It supports lending and valuation purposes. Buyers should use permitted inspections and specialists for condition risks.

faq.question: Can I rely on refinancing later?
faq.answer: No. Future rates, value, income, credit and qualification are uncertain. The original loan should be sustainable.

faq.question: How many lenders should I compare?
faq.answer: Compare multiple written Loan Estimates using matching price, term, lock period and down payment assumptions.

glossary.definition: Final amount due from the buyer after costs, down payment, deposits, credits and adjustments.
Private mortgage insurance that protects a conventional lender against borrower default.
Account used by a servicer to collect and pay specified property taxes and insurance.
Standard disclosure of key terms, projected payments and estimated closing costs for most covered mortgages.
Final disclosure of loan terms and transaction costs generally received before consummation.
Loan balance divided by property value under the applicable definition.
Seller-paid amount toward eligible buyer costs, subject to contract and loan limits.
Upfront charge commonly paid to obtain lower mortgage pricing.
Program charge associated with certain government-backed loans.
Additional charge levied by an association for major costs beyond ordinary dues.
